content: Fish oil is an oil extracted from the tissues of oily fish. It is highly recommended as part of a healthy diet due to its rich content of omega-3 fatty acids, specifically eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). These fatty acids serve as precursors to eicosanoids, which are compounds that help reduce inflammation throughout the body. However, fish themselves do not produce omega-3 fatty acids. Instead, they accumulate these fatty acids by consuming microalgae that produce them, as seen in prey fish like herring and sardines. Predatory fish, such as mackerel, lake trout, albacore tuna, and salmon, obtain omega-3s by eating prey fish that have already accumulated these fatty acids from microalgae. While fatty predatory fish are high in omega-3 fatty acids, they are also at risk of accumulating toxic substances due to their position at the top of the food chain. These toxins include mercury, dioxins, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and chlordane, which can pose health risks. For example, albacore tuna is known to contain high levels of these contaminants. As a result, many individuals turn to fish oil supplements as a safer alternative to obtain adequate omega-3 fatty acids. Fish oil supplements have faced scrutiny in recent years. In early 2006, government agencies such as the UK Food Standards Agency and the Food Safety Authority of Ireland reported that several fish oil brands contained PCB levels exceeding the strict new European maximum limits. This led to the temporary withdrawal of these products from the market. To address concerns about contamination, the International Fish Oil Standards (IFOS) program was established at the University of Guelph as a voluntary review process. Additionally, patented purification processes, known as stripping technology, have been developed to remove pollutants and dioxins from fish oil, reducing them to levels far below European Union limits. Most fish oils used for omega-3 purposes are sourced from regions like Peru, Chile, and Morocco, where fish have higher omega-3 levels (approximately 30%) compared to Scandinavian and other fish oils (around 20%). Fish oils are widely used in the omega-3 industry to produce nutraceuticals and pharmaceuticals. However, the largest consumers of omega-3 fish oils remain the aquaculture feed industry, with major fish feed companies like Ewos, Skretting, and Biomar leading the market. Some experts believe that fish oil consumption, in any form, can help regulate cholesterol levels in the body due to its high omega-3 content. This regulation occurs through the effects of EPA and DHA on peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Beyond cholesterol regulation, fish oil offers anti-inflammatory properties and positive effects on body composition. However, the preferred source of omega-3s should be from the fish's body rather than the liver. Fish liver and liver products, such as cod liver oil, contain omega-3s but also high levels of active vitamin A, which can be toxic at elevated levels. Historical accounts describe early explorers consuming raw liver provided by Inuit natives, leading to vitamin A toxicity in the explorers, while the Inuit, adapted to such diets, remained unaffected. Studies have demonstrated additional benefits of omega-3 fatty acids. For instance, research conducted on prisoners in England showed that higher consumption of omega-3-rich seafood led to a reduction in assault rates. Similarly, a Finnish study found that prisoners convicted of violent crimes had lower omega-3 levels compared to those convicted of nonviolent offenses. It has been suggested that omega-3 fatty acids play a role in neuronal growth in the brain's frontal cortex, which is associated with personal behavior regulation. The American Heart Association recommends a daily intake of 1 gram of fish oil, preferably through fish consumption, for patients with coronary heart disease. The U.S. National Institutes of Health identifies three conditions for which fish oil and other omega-3 sources are most strongly recommended: hypertriglyceridemia, secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease, and high blood pressure. It also lists 27 other conditions for which evidence is less robust. Safety concerns include the potential for increased bleeding risk with omega-3 intakes of 3 grams or more per day, although significant bleeding risks are rare at lower doses. Extremely high intakes, such as those seen in traditional Eskimo diets, may increase the risk of hemorrhagic stroke. A study from Louisiana State University in 2005 suggested that fish oil may help protect the brain from cognitive decline associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Additionally, fish oil has shown promise in aiding the treatment of individuals suffering from depression. When purchasing fish oil dietary supplements, it is highly recommended to look for labels certifying the product as molecularly distilled and USP Certified, ensuring it is free of mercury and other metal toxins.
